section.title: The Man Among the Myrtle Trees
section.sectionRationale: The first of the eight night visions, given on a single night in the eleventh month of Darius's second year, 519 BC. Zechariah sees a rider among the myrtle trees in a ravine, with patrolling horses reporting that all the earth is at rest. The vision answers the community's deepest fear: has God forgotten Jerusalem after seventy years? The angel of the LORD intercedes, and God answers with words of comfort, jealousy for Zion, and the promise to rebuild.
section.thesis: The world may lie deceptively at ease while Zion languishes, but God is not idle or indifferent; He is jealous for Jerusalem, angry with the complacent nations, and He will return with mercy to rebuild His house and comfort His city.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the vision of the rider and patrolling horses reporting the earth at rest; the angel's intercession, how long, and God's comforting words; and the proclamation of God's jealousy for Zion and His promise to return, rebuild, and comfort.

verses.text: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, the month of Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo.
I looked out into the night and saw a man riding on a red horse. He was standing among the {{hadas|myrtle trees}} in the hollow, and behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses.
“What are these, my lord?” I asked. And the angel who was speaking with me replied, “I will show you what they are.”
Then the man standing among the myrtle trees explained, “They are the ones the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.”
And the riders answered the {{malakYHWH|angel of the LORD}} who was standing among the myrtle trees, “We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth is at rest and tranquil.”
Then the angel of the LORD said, “How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which You have been angry these seventy years?”
So the LORD spoke kind and comforting words to the angel who was speaking with me.
Then the angel who was speaking with me said, “Proclaim this word: This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘I am very {{qana|jealous}} for Jerusalem and Zion,
but I am fiercely angry with the nations that are at ease. For I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity.’

Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘I will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and there My house will be rebuilt, declares the LORD of Hosts, and a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem.’
Proclaim further that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘My cities will again overflow with prosperity; the LORD will again {{nacham|comfort}} Zion and choose Jerusalem.’”

hadas.gloss: The myrtle, a modest, fragrant evergreen that grows in low, watered places. Standing in a ravine rather than on a height, the myrtles picture the lowly, unimpressive state of Judah after the exile. Yet the LORD's rider stands among them, a quiet sign that God has not abandoned His humble people.

malakYHWH.gloss: The angel, or messenger, of the LORD. Throughout Zechariah this figure both speaks for God and receives worship-like address, standing among the myrtles and interceding for Jerusalem. Many read this Old Testament figure as a pre-incarnate appearing of the Son, the divine mediator who pleads for God's people.

qana.gloss: To be jealous, zealous, to burn with protective ardor. God's jealousy for Zion is not petty envy but the fierce, faithful love of a husband for his bride. The same zeal that burns against the complacent nations burns for the restoration of His city.

nacham.gloss: To comfort, console, bring relief. God speaks kind and comforting words and promises again to comfort Zion. After seventy years of grief, the covenant word of comfort assures the remnant that God's anger has run its course and His mercy is returning.

basic.context: This is the first of Zechariah's eight night visions, all given on one night in 519 BC. Zechariah sees a rider on a red horse standing among low myrtle bushes in a ravine, with horses that have patrolled the earth and found it peaceful. To a struggling remnant, that peace felt like proof that God had forgotten them. The angel of the LORD asks how long, and God answers with comfort and promises.
basic.hermeneutics: This is apocalyptic vision, so we read the images for their meaning, not as a code to crack detail by detail. People debate exactly who the rider and the angel of the LORD are, and what the patrolling horses represent. But the vision's message is clear: God is watching, He is jealous for Zion, and He will act.
basic.originalLanguages: The rider stands among the hadas, the humble myrtle, a picture of lowly Judah. The malak YHWH, the angel of the LORD, intercedes for Jerusalem. God declares He is qana, jealous, burning with protective love for Zion, and He speaks and promises to nacham, comfort, His grieving city.
basic.typology: The angel of the LORD who stands among the lowly myrtles and pleads for Jerusalem foreshadows Christ, the mediator who dwells with His humble people and intercedes for them. God's promise to return with mercy and rebuild His house points to the greater temple, Christ and His people, and to God dwelling with us.
basic.christ: The angel of the LORD, distinct from yet identified with the LORD, interceding for God's people, points to Jesus, the one mediator who ever lives to intercede for us. The promise I will return to Jerusalem with mercy is fulfilled when God comes near in Christ, and My house will be rebuilt reaches beyond stone to the temple He builds of living stones.
basic.god: God is not distant or indifferent, even when the world seems at ease and His people suffer. He is jealous for His city with a fierce, faithful love, angry with the proud nations who overdid His discipline, and full of mercy and comfort for the afflicted. His silence is never neglect.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 13 and Revelation 6 cry how long. Isaiah 40 and 66 speak God's comfort to Zion. Romans 8 and Hebrews 7 show Christ interceding for His people. Jeremiah 25 and 29 mark the seventy years of exile that this vision brings to an end.
basic.oneStory: In the first night vision God assures a small, discouraged remnant that He sees, He cares, and He is jealous for Zion. His pledge to return with mercy and rebuild runs forward to Christ, the true mediator and temple, and on to the day God dwells fully with His people.

context.literary:
The first night vision is the opening panel of a set of eight, and the set is arranged with care. The horsemen who patrol the earth in 1:8 to 11 return as the four chariots that go out over the earth in 6:1 to 8, so that the whole series begins and ends with riders and horses dispatched by God. Inside that frame the visions are often read in pairs. The horns and craftsmen of 1:18 to 21 answer the removal of wickedness to Babylon in 5:5 to 11. The man with the measuring line in 2:1 to 5 answers the flying scroll of 5:1 to 4. At the centre stand Joshua, the cleansed priest, in chapter 3, and the golden lampstand with Zerubbabel in chapter 4. Whether or not every pairing is intended, the series moves from the world, to Jerusalem, to the leaders, and back out to the world.

Inside this single vision there is a clear movement of speakers. Zechariah sees and asks. The interpreting angel promises to explain. The rider, who is named the angel of the LORD in verse 11, answers. The patrol reports. The angel of the LORD then turns upward and prays, and the LORD answers him. Finally the interpreting angel gives Zechariah four sentences to proclaim, each opening a promise that the previous two verses made necessary: God's jealousy, God's anger with the nations, God's return and rebuilding, God's comfort and choice.

The turn comes in the report of verse 11. The riders announce good news by every ordinary measure, that the whole earth is quiet, and the scene does not treat it as good news. It treats it as the problem. Everything after it is God's answer to a peace that Zion cannot share.

The vision begins at night, verse 8, and its images are muted: myrtles in a hollow, horses of dim colours. The darkness fits a people who could not yet see how things would turn.
context.historical:
The date is the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, in Darius's second year, which falls in January or February of 519 BC by the BSB note. That is exactly two months after Haggai's last oracle, and it is the third of the dated words of this prophetic season, Haggai 2:20 and Zechariah 1:1 having come before it. The temple foundation had been laid and the walls were still down. Judah was a tiny province in a vast empire, and it had little more than the hope that the prophets were speaking for God.

Darius had taken the throne in 522 BC and then spent his first years suppressing revolts in province after province. By 519 the worst was over and the empire was quiet. That is the political setting behind "all the earth is at rest and tranquil." The Persians were also known for their mounted couriers and royal inspectors, officials who rode the roads and reported to the king, and a prophet who watched horsemen report to a higher Lord on the state of the earth was using an image his hearers understood. The empire has its riders. The God of heaven has His.

The seventy years are the other great fact. Jeremiah had foretold that the desolation would last seventy years, Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10, and Daniel 9:2 and 2 Chronicles 36:21 both say they were being fulfilled. Counted from Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC, the period runs to about 519, and the temple was finished in 516, Ezra 6:15. Zechariah 7:5 uses the same round figure of the fasts. The angel's question, "How long?" is asked at the moment the prophesied time is nearly up.

The hearers needed this word because the prophecies of return had begun to come true in a way that looked too small to be real.
context.canonical:
The vision belongs to the biblical tradition of the lament that does not let God go. "How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?" asks Psalm 79:5, and Psalm 90:13 asks, "Return, O LORD! How long will it be?" Psalm 74:10 and the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:10 ask the same. Here the question is put not by a worshipper but by the angel of the LORD, so that the lament of the afflicted is heard in heaven and carried by a mediator.

The answer draws on Isaiah. "Comfort" in Zechariah 1:13 and 1:17 is the verb of Isaiah 40:1, "Comfort, comfort My people," and Isaiah 54:7-8 says almost exactly what the vision says about the proportion of anger and mercy, "For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back." Isaiah 47:6 supplies the charge against the nations, where God says, "I was angry with My people... You showed them no mercy." Joel 2:18, "the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people," shows the pattern of jealousy turning to rescue.

The promises of 1:16 and 1:17 are taken up in the rest of the book. Zechariah 2:1-5 shows the measuring line stretched out over Jerusalem and God Himself as a wall of fire, 2:10-11 has God coming to dwell among His people, 3:1-2 shows the angel of the LORD silencing the accuser, and 8:2-3 repeats the language of jealousy and return almost word for word.

In the New Testament the same strands become the gospel. The intercession of the angel is the pattern of Christ's priestly work, Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34, and God's coming to dwell with His people ends in Revelation 21:3 and 21:22, where the city has no temple because "the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple."

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah wanted a discouraged remnant to understand why their situation looked the way it did, and to learn that the appearance was not the reality. The quiet earth was not a sign that heaven had gone quiet. Behind the calm there are riders reporting to the One who sent them, an intercessor who has taken up the people's lament, and a God who has already moved from anger to comfort.

The author builds the vision so that the comfort comes in the form of an answer to a question the people were afraid to ask. They could hardly have said to God, "How long?" without feeling disloyal, and here the question is put into the mouth of the angel of the LORD and answered with kindness, not rebuke. Lament is therefore authorised. They are allowed to say that seventy years is long enough.

He also wanted them to build. The promise that "My house will be rebuilt" and that a line will be stretched over Jerusalem is not an invitation to wait. It is the assurance that the work of Haggai and Zerubbabel is God's own, so that those who raise stones are in step with Him. The vision makes ordinary labour on a modest building a participation in what God has resolved.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision describes what Zechariah saw and what the LORD said. The details of the scene, the colours of the horses, the number of riders, the hollow where they stand, are the furniture of a vision and not rules. Nothing in the passage tells us how to count or colour them, and the temptation to turn them into a code, matching each colour to a nation or an age, is one the text itself resists by never explaining it.

What is prescriptive is the posture. The vision commands the prophet to "proclaim," and the people to take heart. It also models intercession and lament, which Christians are encouraged to continue, Psalm 79:5 and Revelation 6:10. And it shows how to read an untroubled world: not as proof of God's approval of the world, since God is "fiercely angry with the nations that are at ease," but as a stage on which His purposes are quietly advancing.

The fierce anger toward the nations is God's, not ours. Paul draws the line plainly in Romans 12:19, "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath." The vision teaches believers to place vengeance where it belongs, with the LORD, and to take its comfort in that.

debates.question: Who is the man riding the red horse, and how does he relate to the angel of the LORD?

views.label: The rider is the angel of the LORD
views.case: The man standing among the myrtles in verse 8 is naturally identified with the angel of the LORD standing among the myrtles in verse 11, the divine mediator who then intercedes.

views.label: The rider is the chief of the patrol, distinct from the interpreting angel
views.case: There are at least two angelic figures: the interpreting angel who talks with Zechariah, and the angel of the LORD who intercedes; the rider leads the mounted patrol that reports to him.

debates.bearing: Either way the decisive figure is the angel of the LORD who pleads for Jerusalem, and the vision's comfort does not depend on settling every identification.

debates.question: What does all the earth is at rest and tranquil signify?

views.label: Complacent worldly peace under which Zion still suffers
views.case: The nations are at ease and undisturbed while Jerusalem lies unrestored, which is why God is fiercely angry with the nations that are at ease in verse 15.

views.label: A settled world order that sets the stage for God to act
views.case: The imperial calm after Darius's revolts is the quiet before God moves to restore Zion, so the report prompts the how long that God answers with mercy.

debates.bearing: Both readings expose the same tension: the world's ease is no measure of God's purpose, and God will move to comfort Zion regardless of how settled the nations appear.

debates.question: Which seventy years does the angel have in mind?

views.label: From the first deportation to the return, about 605 to 538 BC
views.case: Jeremiah 25:11 ties the seventy years to the service of Babylon, which began when Nebuchadnezzar rose to power. Daniel 9:2 shows a believer reading the seventy years as nearly done when Babylon's rule ended. On this count the seventy years are over before Zechariah's vision, and the question "how long" concerns the unfinished rebuilding afterward.

views.label: From the destruction of Jerusalem to the rebuilt temple, about 586 to 516 BC
views.case: Zechariah 1:12 says the indignation has lasted "these seventy years," speaking of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. Counting from the burning of the temple in 586 gets to the completion in 516, which is exactly the period of Ezra 6:15. The vision falls near the end, and its promise to rebuild is the answer to the final years.

views.label: A round number for a complete, divinely measured period
views.case: Seventy is often a figure of fullness in the Bible, and 2 Chronicles 36:21 links it to the land's sabbath rests. Read this way the number matters less than the principle that God sets a limit on the discipline.

debates.bearing: The second view fits the wording of the vision most naturally, but the three agree on what matters. The period of judgment is limited by God, and the time to resume mercy had come. The people are not asked to compute the date but to take heart because it has been fixed.

study.originalLanguages:
The question of verse 12, "How long?", is the Hebrew ad matay, the standard lament formula of the Psalms. Psalm 79:5 asks "How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?" and Psalm 90:13 asks "Return, O LORD! How long will it be?" The angel borrows the people's own prayer language. The sentence ends, "with which You have been angry these seventy years," using a verb of indignation, zaam.

The verb that the BSB renders "patrol" in verses 10 and 11 is the reflexive form of the common verb for walking, used for going to and fro. It is the same verb that the book of Job uses when Satan answers God that he has been "walking back and forth" through the earth, Job 1:7. The vocabulary is borrowed from an unsettling place, yet here the riders are God's own patrol and not an adversary's tour. The comparison highlights the difference. In Job the one who walks the earth is the accuser. In Zechariah the riders are sent by the LORD, and the angel of the LORD takes the people's side.

"At rest and tranquil" renders two roots, yashab, to sit, and shaqat, to be quiet. Isaiah 14:7 uses the same root of the earth's relief when the Babylonian tyrant has fallen: "All the earth is at peace and at rest." In Isaiah the quiet is the sound of oppression ending. In Zechariah the quiet falls while the oppressed are still in the hollow. The same word marks two opposite situations, which is why the angel cannot rest in it.

The accusation against the nations in verse 15 turns on one verb. God says He was angry "a little," but "they have added to the calamity." The Hebrew behind "added to" is azar, the ordinary word for "help." The nations helped, but toward evil. They took a limited discipline and made it a rout. That is why the BSB footnote offers "Or they have overdone the punishment." The same word that usually describes assistance records an assistance God never asked for.

In verse 16 the promise "I will return to Jerusalem" is literally in the perfect tense, "I have returned." The prophet speaks of God's return as already begun, and the verb is the same shub as the "return" of the previous study's call in 1:3. God's return answers the people's. The accompanying noun for "mercy" is rachamim, plural, from the same root as the word for womb. It is the compassion of a mother for the child of her body. And the promise that God's "good words" and "comforting words" were spoken in verse 13 is plural twice, as if the answer to seventy years of anger had to be given in many sentences.

Finally, in verse 17 the verb for cities that will "overflow with prosperity" comes from a root that often means to scatter. Judah has been scattered, but goodness is the thing that will now spill out of the cities.

typology.type: The angel of the LORD interceding for Jerusalem
typology.fulfillment: The angel stands before the LORD of Hosts and asks for mercy on a people that cannot ask for itself. In Christ the pattern becomes a person: "He always lives to intercede for them," Hebrews 7:25, and He is "interceding for us," Romans 8:34. He appears "on our behalf in the presence of God," Hebrews 9:24, and is our "advocate before the Father," 1 John 2:1. The type falls short because the angel pleads from outside the suffering, while Christ pleads as the high priest who "was tempted in every way that we are," Hebrews 4:15.

typology.type: The rider among the myrtles in the hollow
typology.fulfillment: The angel of the LORD stands among the humble bushes in the low place, with the people of the hollow. The correspondence in Christ is His presence among His people. He is the One who "walks among the seven golden lampstands," Revelation 2:1, whom John sees "among the lampstands," Revelation 1:13, and who promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them," Matthew 18:20. The type is limited by its mystery. The vision does not tell us who the rider is, while the New Testament names Him.

typology.type: God's return to Jerusalem with mercy
typology.fulfillment: The promise "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy" has a first fulfilment in the rebuilt temple and a larger one when God comes in person. Zacharias blesses the Lord for having "visited and redeemed His people," Luke 1:68, and John writes that the Word "made His dwelling among us," John 1:14. The final form is Revelation 21:3, "the dwelling place of God is with man." The type is partial because the second temple lacked the glory of the first, while the dwelling of Christ with His people is permanent.

The answer to the angel's prayer is comfort. Simeon is described as "waiting for the consolation of Israel," Luke 2:25, and he finds it in the infant Jesus. Paul calls God "the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort," 2 Corinthians 1:3. The comfort of the vision is a promise about circumstances, while the comfort of the gospel includes the removal of sin, which is why Isaiah 40:2 ties comfort to pardon. The type points to what the word was waiting for.

study.christ:
The vision leads to Christ most plainly through its central figure. The man among the myrtles is identified in verse 11 as the angel of the LORD, a figure who runs through the Old Testament. He speaks as God and is yet distinguished from God. In Genesis 16:7-13 he finds Hagar and promises her descendants, and Hagar calls the LORD who spoke to her "the God who sees me." In Exodus 3:2-6 he appears in the burning bush, and the voice from it says, "I am the God of your father." In Judges 6:11-14 he sits under the oak and then "the LORD turned to him." Zechariah 3:1-2 shows him next to the high priest in a scene where "the LORD rebukes you, Satan." Many of the church fathers and later theologians recognised in this figure the Son of God before His coming in flesh, one who is sent and yet is the LORD. Others read him as the highest of the angels who speaks in the divine name. The vision does not settle the matter, but it supplies the pattern that the New Testament makes explicit: the one who pleads with God for His people also speaks for God to them.

That pattern becomes Christ's priesthood. "He always lives to intercede for them," Hebrews 7:25. "Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and He is interceding for us," Romans 8:34. The angel asks how long, and the Son has already supplied the reason the answer can be mercy, because He has borne the anger that lay on the people. The comfort of Isaiah 40:2, "her iniquity has been pardoned," rests on that work.

The vision leads to Christ by its theme of God's return. "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy" is fulfilled, in the New Testament's own telling, when "God sent His Son," Galatians 4:4, and when Zacharias sings that God "has visited and redeemed His people," Luke 1:68. Jesus Himself connects the visit to Jerusalem: "you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God," Luke 19:44. The promise that "My house will be rebuilt" He fulfils in a way the builders of 519 could not guess, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again," John 2:19, speaking "about the temple of His body," 2:21. His followers are then "like living stones, being built into a spiritual house," 1 Peter 2:5.

God's jealousy for Zion is also taken up in Him. When Jesus drives the traders from the temple, His disciples remember, "Zeal for Your house will consume Me," John 2:17. The jealous love that burned for the city burns in the Son.

A caution is needed. The horses, their colours and the myrtle grove are not codes for Christ. The link is carried by the figure of the mediating angel and by the promises of return and comfort, and by the New Testament's own use of the themes. Where the vision is quiet, the reader should be too.
study.god:
The vision first shows a God who knows. The riders are sent to cover the earth, and they report to the angel of the LORD. Zechariah 4:10 later calls the seven eyes of the LORD those that "scan the whole earth." Nothing about the quiet of the nations goes unseen. The comfort of the vision is that the people are not hidden from heaven.

It shows a God who hears and answers. The angel's question in verse 12 is not rebuked. The very next verse says the LORD "spoke kind and comforting words," and the Bible does not record any hesitation. The contrast with the people's fear that their prayers went nowhere is deliberate. God had not stopped listening. The question had been heard before it was asked, and the answer was already in motion. This is not a God who must be argued into mercy, since the angel's prayer follows God's own purposes and is answered because it agrees with them.

It shows a God whose anger has limits and a purpose. He says, "I was a little angry," and the weight of the sentence lies on "a little." Isaiah 54:8 uses the same measure: "In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you." The anger is real, since the seventy years were not imaginary, but it is the anger of a father disciplining, and it is outweighed by what follows. The nations that took God's discipline as licence are another matter. They are the object of an anger that is described as "fierce," and Isaiah 10:5-7 explains the principle, that the instruments of God's judgment are held to account for their own pride.

It shows a God who is jealous. "I am very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion" is the speech of a covenant husband, in the tradition of Exodus 20:5, "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God." Jealousy in this sense is not insecurity but exclusive love that will not let a beloved be destroyed. Joel 2:18 shows the same love moving God to spare, and Zechariah 8:2 repeats it.

It shows a God who chooses again. "The LORD will again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem" promises that the election has not lapsed. Zechariah 2:12 and Zechariah 3:2 repeat it, so the choice rests on God's grace and not on the people's record.

Finally, it shows God holding two things that often seem opposed. He is sovereign over the quiet nations and the unquiet people, and He is also moved to compassion. The vision does not resolve the tension by shrinking either side. It lets the angel's prayer and God's decision stand together, as the Bible's doctrine of providence does throughout.

For worship, the vision permits honest lament and commands confident trust. The seventy years of silence were not abandonment. The believer who prays "How long?" is joining a prayer that has already been taken up in heaven and answered with kindness.

crossReferences.note: God promises that when Babylon's seventy years are complete He will attend to His people and bring them back. Zechariah 1:12 shows that the period is now being measured against that word, and the angel's "how long" is asked within a promise that has an end date.

Satan comes before the LORD from "roaming through the earth," and the verse for his "walking back and forth" is the same verb Zechariah uses for the riders' patrol. The contrast shows that in the heavenly court Zechariah describes, the ones who walk the earth are sent by the LORD, and their report is heard by a mediator.

"How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever? Will Your jealousy burn like fire?" is the prayer of a people in ruins. The angel's question gives the prayer to heaven's own intercessor, and God's jealousy, which the psalmist feared, becomes in Zechariah the very thing that rescues.

The word "comfort" in Zechariah 1:13 and 1:17 is the verb of Isaiah's opening call to comfort God's people because her service is complete and her iniquity pardoned. Zechariah applies the Isaiah promise to the rebuilding generation.

God says He forsook His people for a brief moment and hid His face in a surge of anger, but will bring them back with great compassion. The proportion of a little anger and a long mercy is the same one the LORD states in Zechariah 1:15-16.

God tells Babylon that He was angry with His people and gave them into her hand, but she showed them no mercy. It is the clearest background for Zechariah 1:15, where the nations are accused of adding to the calamity beyond what God intended.

The next vision shows the measuring line promised in 1:16 and takes the promise further: Jerusalem will have no walls because of its multitude, and God will be a wall of fire around it and the glory within it. The promise to rebuild opens into the promise of a protected, overflowing city.

The angel of the LORD appears again, now standing beside Joshua the high priest while Satan accuses. The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebukes Satan. The scene shows what the intercession of chapter 1 looks like in action, with the accuser silenced and a guilty man rescued.

Christ "always lives to intercede" for those who draw near to God through Him. The interceding angel of Zechariah 1:12 finds its fullest answer here, because the Son pleads not as a visitor but as the high priest whose own offering secures the answer.

The souls under the altar cry, "How long, O Lord, holy and true," and are told to rest a little longer. The question of Zechariah 1:12 is still being asked at the end of the age, and the answer is the same: God hears, and He has set a number and a time.

The final fulfilment of "I will return to Jerusalem." God dwells with His people in a city whose temple is the Lord God and the Lamb. The mercy that began as the rebuilding of one small house ends as the dwelling of God with humanity.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is full of times when the world seems to carry on regardless of God's people. Egypt prospers while Israel groans. Babylon feasts while Jerusalem burns. In each case the people ask how long, and in each case the answer, however slow, comes. Zechariah's first vision places that question at a very particular point: the end of the exile, in a quiet that does not look like freedom.

Behind the vision lies the covenant. God had promised Abraham a people, a land and a blessing, Genesis 12:1-3, and had given His presence among them in the tabernacle and the temple. The exile appeared to undo it all, and Zechariah's hearers knew the story of how it happened. The vision does not deny the cause. It says God was angry a little, and that His anger has been turned by a love that never stopped being jealous for Zion.

It also sets up what comes next in Zechariah. The measuring line, the cleansing of the high priest, the lampstand and the closing scenes of kings and shepherds all grow from the promise made here: "I will return to Jerusalem with mercy." The book keeps that promise in view all the way to the closing chapter, where the LORD will be king over all the earth, Zechariah 14:9.

The New Testament tells how the return came. God did not simply rebuild a building. He sent His Son, who is the true Presence, the temple raised in three days, and the intercessor who always lives to plead for His own. Jesus' lament over Jerusalem, "how often I have longed to gather your children together," Matthew 23:37, shows the same jealous love in His own voice.

In the new creation the question "How long?" is finally answered. The martyrs, told to rest a little longer, Revelation 6:11, see the end of the world's calm and of its cruelty. The city is measured, Revelation 21:15, God dwells with His people, and the nations that once sat at ease have their place in it, since "by its light the nations will walk," Revelation 21:24. The night in which Zechariah saw the riders gives way to a city where "there will be no more night," Revelation 22:5.

quiz.q: What did the patrolling horses report about the earth?

options.text: That all the earth was at rest and tranquil, while Zion still lay unrestored.
options.note: Verse 11 reports the world at ease, which sharpens the angel's how long.

options.text: That the whole earth was in violent upheaval.
options.note: The report is of calm, not chaos; the tension is that the world is settled while Zion suffers.

options.text: That Jerusalem was already fully rebuilt.
options.note: Jerusalem still awaited restoration, which is why God promises to return with mercy.

options.text: That the horses had failed to find anything.
options.note: They completed their patrol and gave a clear report.

quiz.q: What does God's jealousy for Zion mean in this vision?

options.text: His fierce, faithful covenant love for Jerusalem, burning for her good and against the nations that harmed her.
options.note: Verses 14-15 show qana as protective, zealous love, not petty envy.

options.text: A childish resentment that others have more than He does.
options.note: God's jealousy is holy covenant love, not the sinful envy the word can mean among people.

options.text: Indifference toward what happens to Jerusalem.
options.note: Jealousy here is the opposite of indifference; God is deeply invested in Zion.

options.text: Anger directed only at His own people.
options.note: His fierce anger falls on the complacent nations; His jealousy burns for Zion's good.

quiz.q: How does the angel of the LORD function in this vision?

options.text: As a mediator who intercedes for Jerusalem, asking God how long He will withhold mercy.
options.note: Verse 12 shows the angel pleading for God's afflicted people.

options.text: As an accuser demanding Jerusalem's destruction.
options.note: The accuser appears later in chapter 3; here the angel intercedes on Jerusalem's behalf.

options.text: As a silent observer with no role.
options.note: The angel actively intercedes and relays God's comforting answer.

options.text: As one of the enemy nations.
options.note: The angel stands for God's people, not against them.

quiz.q: What does God promise to do for Jerusalem?

options.text: Return with mercy, rebuild His house, and again comfort Zion and choose Jerusalem.
options.note: Verses 16-17 gather God's promises of mercy, rebuilding, and comfort.

options.text: Leave the city in ruins as a lasting monument to judgment.
options.note: The opposite: God promises restoration and overflowing prosperity.

options.text: Hand Jerusalem over permanently to the nations.
options.note: God turns against the nations and returns to His city with mercy.

options.text: Forget His covenant with the city forever.
options.note: God renews His choice of Jerusalem rather than abandoning it.

quiz.q: How does this vision point forward to Christ?

options.text: The angel of the LORD interceding foreshadows Christ our mediator, and I will return with mercy anticipates God drawing near in Him.
options.note: Christ is the one mediator who intercedes, and God with us in the incarnation.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: The interceding mediator and God's promised return both lead to Christ.

options.text: It teaches that God no longer dwells with His people.
options.note: It promises the opposite, God returning to dwell with them, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It proves the temple would never be rebuilt.
options.note: God promises His house will be rebuilt, pointing beyond stone to Christ.

questions: The world lay at ease while Zion suffered. When the wicked seem comfortable and you feel forgotten, how does it help to know God is jealous for His people?
The angel of the LORD prayed how long for Jerusalem. What are the how long prayers you are carrying, and how does Christ's intercession give you confidence to keep praying?
God stood among the lowly myrtles, not on a mountain height. How does it comfort you that God draws near to the humble and discouraged rather than the self-satisfied?
God promised to comfort Zion after seventy long years. Where do you need to trust that God's discipline has a limit and His mercy is returning?
My house will be rebuilt points forward to God dwelling with His people in Christ. How does the hope of God dwelling with you shape your endurance now?

translationNotes.note: Myrtle trees renders hadas, a low, fragrant evergreen of watered valleys; standing in the hollow, the myrtles picture lowly, restored Judah among whom the LORD's rider still stands.
Jealous renders qana, a burning, protective covenant love; the same zeal flames for Zion and, in verse 15, against the complacent nations.
They have added to the calamity: a footnote records the alternative they have overdone the punishment; the nations went beyond God's measured discipline of Judah.
